title.en: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

text.en: Ravi opens his lunch box and finds roti, dal, vegetables and a banana. Which part gives him energy, which helps him grow and which keeps him healthy? Let us look at food closely.

Different regions of India have different foods. Many ingredients come from plants or animals, while mushrooms come from fungi. Water and salt come from other sources. Food gives us energy, helps us grow and repair our bodies and keeps us healthy.
The main components are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Carbohydrates, such as in rice and roti, give energy. Proteins, in dal, eggs and milk, help growth and repair. Fats, such as those in ghee and oil, provide energy. Vitamins and minerals help the body work properly. Fibre helps digestion and water keeps the body working.
Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present. A paper rubbed with a food that contains fat shows an oily patch that stays when dry. Testing helps us find what a food contains.
A balanced diet has all the components in the right amount. Getting too little of some nutrients over time can lead to deficiency problems. For example, a long-term lack of vitamin C can cause bleeding gums, although bleeding gums can have other causes. A food can provide plenty of energy but little fibre or few vitamins. One snack alone does not tell us how varied a person’s meals are.
Millets such as ragi and jowar are cereals rich in nutrients that grow with little water. Food miles measure how far food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten. Food from nearby often travels a shorter distance. Freshness also depends on time, handling and storage.
Eat slowly, chew well, avoid wasting food and wash your hands before eating. Choose fresh and home cooked meals and drink enough water.

Rice, roti and ragi preparations look and taste different. All begin with grains from plants. A food list can show both the variety of meals and the ingredients they have in common.
Food rarely fits into a single nutrient box. Dal supplies protein and also contains carbohydrates and fibre. A category tells us one contribution of a food.
Two sample food labels list protein per hundred grams. The first shows four grams and the second shows seven. Because we are comparing equal amounts of food, the second lists more protein.

board.text: Per 100 g: compare 4 g and 7 g

text.en: What if one label showed a thirty-gram serving and the other a hundred grams? Compare the same amount on both labels before drawing a conclusion about their protein content.
Imagine watching a teacher demonstrate the iodine test. The teacher labels a known starch sample and a plain water sample so the class can compare the results. Do not taste any test sample.
If the sample containing starch turns blue-black and the plain water does not, the water gives us a comparison. We can then look for the same colour change in a food sample.

board.text: Blue-black is the sign we look for

text.en: A class can also compare an oily mark and a water mark on paper. Once it dries, the water mark usually disappears. A patch made by oil may still look translucent.
Each classroom test looks for a clue about one component. A starch test does not tell us how much protein a food contains, and an oily patch does not measure all its nutrients.
Think of two imaginary lunch boxes with different grains, pulses and vegetables. You can compare what food groups they contain, even when none of the dishes are identical.
Some foods can contribute particular vitamins or minerals. Guava contains vitamin C, for example, while milk can provide calcium. A varied food list helps us notice different contributions.
Ragi and jowar are examples of millets. Families can turn these grains into different foods, such as flatbreads or porridge. The same crop can appear in many regional meals.
A crop travels twelve kilometres from a farm to a market and another three kilometres to school. Add both legs of the journey when you work out the food miles.
Suppose another delivery comes from farther away but arrives sooner. Its distance is still longer. To compare freshness, we would need more information, such as when the food was picked.
Pick one familiar dish and tell a partner about one ingredient, one nutrient it supplies, and one question you could ask about its journey to your plate.

problem.en: Which food group does dal belong to?

text.en: Dal is rich in protein.
So it is a protein food.

why.en: Group dal by an important nutrient it supplies. Dal has other nutrients too.

prompt.en: Explain why a balanced diet is better than eating only one kind of food.

requiredIdeas.en: Different foods provide these components in different amounts.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking only energy foods are needed.

points.en: Food gives energy, growth and protection.
Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water.
Millets and local foods are good choices.
